title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
prompt:
Given the `root` of a binary tree (not necessarily a BST) and two values `p` and `q` that both exist in the tree (values are unique), return the **value** of their lowest common ancestor. A node can be an ancestor of itself.

The helpers `TreeNode` and `build(levelOrderArray)` are provided; tests call e.g. `lowestCommonAncestor(build([3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4]), 5, 1)`.

**Example:** p=5, q=1 -> `3`; p=5, q=4 -> `5`.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion stack
hints: Recurse: what should a subtree report back to its parent?
Return the node if it matches p or q, otherwise whatever non-null result the children produced.
If both children return non-null, the current node is the split point: the LCA.
keyPoints: Post-order recursion returning the found node or null
Split point where left and right both non-null is the LCA
Handles a node being its own ancestor by returning early on match
Mention BST variant (walk by value) and parent-pointer variant (ancestor set)
Discuss recursion depth on skewed trees; iterative with parent map if needed

title: Serialize and Deserialize a Binary Tree
prompt:
Implement `serialize(root)` that turns a binary tree into a string and `deserialize(str)` that rebuilds the identical tree. The format is up to you, but it must round-trip any tree, including empty trees, negative values and skewed shapes.

Helpers `TreeNode`, `build(arr)` and `toArr(root)` are provided; tests check `toArr(deserialize(serialize(build([...]))))` equals the original level-order array.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for both operations
hints: Preorder alone is ambiguous; what extra token makes it unambiguous?
Emit a sentinel (e.g. '#') for every null child.
Deserialize by consuming tokens recursively in the same preorder sequence.
keyPoints: Preorder with null markers uniquely encodes a tree
Delimiter choice must handle negative and multi-digit values
Recursive or iterative token consumption with a shared index/queue
Alternative BFS level-order encoding; trim trailing nulls
Discuss recursion depth limits for very deep trees and versioning the wire format

title: Shortest Path in a Binary Matrix
prompt:
Given an `n x n` grid of 0s (open) and 1s (blocked), return the length (number of cells) of the shortest clear path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, moving in any of **8 directions**. Return `-1` if no path exists (including when start or end is blocked).

**Example:** `shortestPathBinaryMatrix([[0,1],[1,0]])` -> `2`
hints: Unweighted shortest path suggests BFS, not DFS.
Process level by level; each level is one more cell in the path.
Mark cells visited when you enqueue them, not when you dequeue, to avoid duplicates.
keyPoints: BFS gives shortest path in an unweighted graph
Check blocked start/end up front
Mark visited on enqueue
8-directional neighbours
Mention A* with Chebyshev heuristic as an optimisation

title: Edit Distance
prompt:
Given strings `a` and `b`, return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions or substitutions needed to turn `a` into `b`.

**Example:** `minDistance("horse", "ros")` -> `3`
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(n) with rolling rows
hints: Define dp[i][j] = cost to convert the first i chars of a into the first j chars of b.
If the chars match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min of replace, delete, insert.
Base cases: converting to/from an empty prefix costs its length. Only the previous row is needed.
keyPoints: Clear state definition over prefixes
Three transitions: substitute, delete, insert
Base row/column initialised to indices
Space optimisation to O(min(m,n))
Can reconstruct the edit script by backtracking a full table

title: Coin Change (Fewest Coins)
prompt:
Given coin denominations `coins` (unlimited supply of each) and an `amount`, return the fewest coins needed to make that amount, or `-1` if impossible.

**Example:** `coinChange([1,2,5], 11)` -> `3` (5+5+1)
hints: Greedy (largest coin first) fails for coins like [1,3,4] and amount 6.
dp[x] = fewest coins to make x; dp[0] = 0.
dp[x] = min over coins c <= x of dp[x - c] + 1; unreachable stays Infinity.
keyPoints: Show a counterexample to greedy
Bottom-up unbounded knapsack recurrence
Sentinel for unreachable amounts, guard against overflow in Java
Amount 0 returns 0
BFS over amounts is an equivalent alternative

title: String to Integer (atoi)
prompt:
Implement `myAtoi(s)`:

1. Skip leading spaces.
2. Read an optional `+` or `-`.
3. Read digits until a non-digit or end of string; ignore the rest.
4. If no digits were read, return `0`.
5. Clamp to the 32-bit signed range `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`.

**Example:** `myAtoi("   -42abc")` -> `-42`
hints: Write the steps as a tiny state machine: spaces, sign, digits.
Stop at the first non-digit after the optional sign.
Check overflow as you accumulate, before the value grows unbounded.
keyPoints: Clarify the spec and enumerate edge cases before coding
Only one sign character allowed
Clamp on overflow, detected during accumulation
Avoid returning -0 in JS
In Java use long or pre-check MAX/10 to avoid overflow

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
prompt:
Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the nodes `k` at a time and return the new head. If the number of remaining nodes is less than `k`, leave them as they are. Rewire nodes; do not just swap values.

Helpers `ListNode`, `fromList(arr)` and `toList(head)` are provided.

**Example:** `toList(reverseKGroup(fromList([1,2,3,4,5]), 2))` -> `[2,1,4,3,5]`
hints: A dummy head removes the special case for the first group.
Before reversing, walk k steps to confirm a full group exists.
Reverse the group pointing its tail at the next group's head, then reconnect the previous group.
keyPoints: Dummy node and groupPrev pointer
Check a full group exists before mutating
In-place reversal with prev initialised to groupNext
Reconnect: groupPrev.next = kth, advance groupPrev to old first
O(1) extra space; recursive version uses O(n/k) stack

title: Spiral Matrix
prompt:
Given an `m x n` matrix, return all elements in clockwise spiral order starting from the top-left.

**Example:** `spiralOrder([[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]])` -> `[1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5]`
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(1) besides output
hints: Track four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
Traverse one edge, then shrink that boundary.
Guard the bottom and left passes so single rows/columns are not visited twice.
keyPoints: Boundary-shrinking simulation
Guards for non-square and single row/column cases
Handle empty input
Alternative: direction vector with visited markers
Each element visited exactly once
